title: Crossing the Rhône
summary: Force the Rhône against the Volcae massed on the far bank - by bridge or by raft, with Hanno's detachment falling on them from upstream - then capture two Roman advance camps before Scipio reaches the river.
teaching_goal: A camp is taken by standing in it, not by levelling it. A dozen companies cannot kill fifty, but they can hold two gate yards long enough to claim them - and a Roman column without its commander stops being a column.
narrative_intent: A broad river operation with ferries, wooded detours, bridgeheads, and fortified supply quarters: the Volcae hold the far end of the crossing, Hanno's Iberians wait upstream on their side of the water, and the Iron Sepulcher occupies an avoidable ruin on the southern flank.
historical_context: 218 BC: Hannibal reached the Rhône some four days' march from the sea and found the Volcae massed on the east bank to stop him. He sent Hanno son of Bomilcar upstream by night with a picked force, mostly Iberians; they crossed on rafts and skins, came down the far bank and signalled with smoke. As the boats and rafts pushed off, Hanno fell on the Volcae from behind and broke them. The elephants were floated over on earth-covered rafts, and Scipio's scouting horse clashed with the Numidians before the consul, landed at the river mouth, arrived three days too late (Polybius 3.42-49; Livy 21.26-32). Historical: the Volcae, Hanno's flanking march, the rafts and elephants, the cavalry skirmish. Altered: the bridges, the Roman advance camps on the far-bank road and Scipio's garrisons - Rome had no army at the crossing - and the Iron Sepulcher's barrows.

victory_conditions.description: Seize the hill fort and the river town. Leave no crossing for Scipio's army to inherit.
Kill every enemy commander. A nation dies with the man who leads it: its camps fall neutral, its works come down and its troops leave the field.

defeat_conditions.description: Every soldier lost is counted by the enemy tonight.
The commander falls — and every line collapses behind him.
A general alone on a dead field is just the last corpse standing.

optional_objectives.description: Break the barrow-guard south of the camp. The dead keep gold no Roman has counted.

stages.title: Reach the Rhone crossing
stages.description: Bring the column to the pontoon bridge on the near bank. The Volcae hold its far end.
stages.hint: The river runs north to south across the middle of the valley; the nearest crossing is due east of camp. Hanno's Iberians wait upstream on the far bank - strike the Volcae from both sides at once.

stages.title: Seize the Roman hill fort
stages.description: Stand in the gate yard of the northern advance camp until it falls to Carthage.
stages.hint: A camp is taken by holding its yard, not by levelling it.

stages.title: Seize the river town
stages.description: Take the second camp on the southern supply road. No bridge reaches its bank of the river.
stages.hint: Ferry your companies over on the rafts, one at a time - the elephants too, as Hannibal floated his across: one below the Gaulish landing, one further south, one across the eastern branch.

stages.title: Kill the Roman commanders
stages.description: A column without its commander stops being a column.
stages.hint: Enemy camps fall neutral once their commander is dead.

actions.text: The Rhône runs north to south through the valley. Roman pickets watch every approach on the near bank.
Six bridges span the Rhône, and Roman eyes watch the far end of every one. Pick a crossing and commit.
Two camps hold the far bank: a hill fort to the north-east, a walled river town far to the south-east. Stand in their gate yards to take them.
Smoke on the far bank, upstream of the bridge. Hanno son of Bomilcar crossed by night on rafts and skins with his Iberians; the Volcae watching the crossing have not seen him.

commander_messages.speaker: roman_veteran_consul
commander_messages.text: So. The Barcid crawls down to the Rhone. Cross where you like - the river is not particular about whose bones it keeps, and Rome has a great deal of patience and a very great many shovels. My surveyors are already pacing out your grave. They tell me the ground here drinks well.

commander_messages.speaker: roman_veteran_consul
commander_messages.text: You have the river town. My congratulations - you now own three hundred mouths, two wells, and a temple whose god has lately been asking after Carthage by name. Feed them. I shall come back in the spring and count what is left.

commander_messages.speaker: roman_legion_organizer
commander_messages.text: You killed a consul. Good. Rome keeps forty more in cupboards in the city, and I promise you the ones still in the cupboards are worse. He will be missed - briefly, and only by his creditors.

commander_messages.speaker: roman_veteran_consul
commander_messages.text: Take the crossings, then. Take the whole cold length of the road north and every stone laid on it. Rome does not lose provinces - she lends them, at interest, and I am told the collectors on this road wear no faces at all.

commander_messages.speaker: roman_veteran_consul
commander_messages.text: There. Sit down in the mud with the others. They tell me the men who die on this road do not stay where they are put - that they rise about the third watch and go on marching north without their officers. Do continue. You are expected.

commander_messages.speaker: roman_legion_organizer
commander_messages.text: The hill fort is yours. It was built to watch a river; now it will watch you cross one. Forts do not much care who is inside them.

commander_messages.speaker: roman_veteran_consul
commander_messages.text: My scouting party is on the road. Cavalry, mostly, and a tribune who wants to be noticed. Do notice him.

commander_messages.speaker: roman_veteran_consul
commander_messages.text: Patrols at your works. You are trying to cross a river with your back to my roads. It is bold. It is also how one drowns.

commander_messages.speaker: roman_veteran_consul
commander_messages.text: Your men are falling at the water. The Rhone is not particular about whose bones it keeps; I did tell you.

commander_messages.speaker: roman_veteran_consul
commander_messages.text: Hannibal falls at the Rhône. Then Rome never sees the elephants, and no one ever learns the name Cannae. I shall spend the rest of my life not knowing what I was spared.

commander_messages.speaker: roman_veteran_consul
commander_messages.text: The patrols are nearly finished. So be it. I shall take the fleet back to Italy and wait for you there with the rest of the Republic.

commander_messages.speaker: carthage_sword_commander
commander_messages.text: Hanno's smoke is up on the far bank. His Iberians are behind the Volcae - across, all of you, while they look the wrong way. Scipio is three days behind and I intend to keep him there.

commander_messages.speaker: carthage_sword_commander
commander_messages.text: Their scouts have seen us. Good. Let them ride back and tell Scipio what they saw.

commander_messages.speaker: carthage_sword_commander
commander_messages.text: The fort is ours. Hold the gate - its barracks will give us the men the river took.

theme: The river is wide, the far bank is guarded, and every minute standing still costs blood.
